label: Organisms grow along stream lines definable by a mathematical transformation
statement: The law of growth implied by representing related forms as orthogonal coordinate transformations is that the organism grows along stream lines definable by a suitable mathematical transformation; departures from orthogonality reflect the organism not being homogeneous and isotropic.
quote: the “law of growth” which our biological analysis by means of orthogonal co-ordinate systems presupposes, or at least foreshadows, is one according to which the organism grows or develops along _stream lines_, which may be defined by a suitable mathematical transformation.
scope: growth of organisms in general

label: Many organic forms arise from uniform expansive growth limited by local constraints
statement: Many developmental changes of form are produced by local trammels or lines of constraint acting on otherwise uniform and symmetrical expansive growth, as a ligature turns a gourd into two globes or a muscular band makes the stomach a lopsided bubble.
quote: It is clear, I think, that we may account for many ordinary biological processes of development or transformation of form by the existence of trammels or lines of constraint, which limit and determine the action of the expansive forces of growth that would otherwise be uniform and symmetrical.
scope: development of tubular and vesicular organs (gut, stomach, heart, neural tube) and fruits

label: One transformation accounts for all external differences between porcupine-fish and sunfish
statement: Deforming the coordinate grid of Diodon (concentric circles and approximately hyperbolic curves) yields the outline of the sunfish Orthagoriscus, so that a single integral transformation accounts for all their apparently separate external differences while leaving the head region nearly unchanged.
quote: And as such it accounts, by one single integral transformation, for all the apparently separate and distinct external differences between the two fishes.
scope: Diodon and Orthagoriscus (Mola), and by extension related fish genera

label: One harmonious deformation accounts for all skull differences among crocodilians
statement: Across most crocodilian genera, the skull contours and even the shapes and sizes of individual bones and vacuities can be derived from one another by a single simple coordinate transformation, so that the skull of Notosuchus can be reconstructed bone for bone from that of Crocodilus.
quote: To all intents and purposes, then, this not very complex system, representing one harmonious “deformation,” accounts for _all_ the differences between the two figures, and is sufficient to enable one at any time to reconstruct a detailed drawing, bone for bone, of the skull of _Notosuchus_ from the model furnished by the common crocodile.
scope: skulls of crocodilians, living and fossil (excluding the oldest forms such as Belodon)

label: Fossil horse skulls match interpolated stages between Hyracotherium and Equus
statement: Skulls interpolated by coordinate transformation between Hyracotherium (Eohippus) and Equus coincide closely with actual fossil skulls of Mesohippus and Protohippus, which therefore lie on the transformation series from Eohippus to the horse.
quote: it will be seen that the actual fossil skull coincides in the most perfect fashion with one of the hypothetical forms or stages which our method shews to be implicitly involved in the transition from _Hyracotherium_ to _Equus_.
scope: skulls of fossil and living Equidae

label: Parahippus is a divergent offshoot, not on the direct line to Equus
statement: Because the skull of Parahippus fits the interpolated transformation series from Eohippus to Equus poorly, Parahippus is not in the direct line of descent but represents a divergent branch of the Equidae.
quote: In short, though some writers have placed _Parahippus_ in the direct line of descent between _Equus_ and _Eohippus_, we see at once that there is no place for it there, and that it must, accordingly, represent a somewhat divergent branch or offshoot of the Equidae.
scope: phylogeny of fossil Equidae

label: Perissodactyls are more closely related to hares and rabbits than to other ungulates
statement: Since the rabbit's skull is derived from that of a primitive rhinoceros by a simple uniform downward flexure, the Perissodactyla are more closely related to the Leporidae than to other ungulates, and the Leporidae more closely to Perissodactyla than to other rodents.
quote: For my part, I would go further; for I think there is strong reason to believe that the Perissodactyles are more closely related to the Leporidae than the former are to the other Ungulates, or than the Leporidae are to the rest of the Rodentia.
scope: phylogenetic relationships of Perissodactyla, Leporidae, other ungulates and rodents

label: Ape and human skull differences form one continuous, roughly logarithmic transformation
statement: The differences between the human skull and the skulls of the chimpanzee and baboon form one continuous integral deformation in which corresponding areas of the grid increase approximately logarithmically downwards and forwards, rather than separate modifications of jaws, braincase and face.
quote: In both dimensions, as we pass from above downwards and from behind forwards, the corresponding areas of the network are seen to increase in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order in the lower as compared with the higher type of skull; and, in short, it becomes at once manifest that the modifications of jaws, braincase, and the regions between are all portions of one continuous and integral process.
scope: skulls of humans and anthropoid primates

label: Human and anthropoid skulls show divergent rather than linear evolutionary change
statement: No continuous transformation series passes through known fossil and living human and anthropoid skulls (Mesopithecus, Pithecanthropus, Neanderthal, modern man), indicating that there is no single straight line of descent and that their variation has been divergent.
quote: The failure is not the fault of our method. It merely indicates that no one straight line of descent, or of consecutive transformation, exists; but on the contrary, that among human and anthropoid types, recent and extinct, we have to do with a complex problem of divergent, rather than of continuous, variation.
scope: fossil and living hominids and anthropoid apes

label: Depth expansion and lateral compression vary inversely, conserving fish volume
statement: In related fishes, expansion in one transverse dimension tends to be compensated by compression in the other, so that volume at a given length changes less than linear dimensions; the plaice is about twice as deep and half as thick as the haddock and has almost the same length-weight coefficient k = W/L^3.
quote: the very fact that the two dimensions tend to vary _inversely_ already assures us that, in the general process of deformation, the _volume_ is less affected than are the _linear dimensions_.
scope: related fish species differing in body depth and width (e.g. haddock and plaice, shark and skate)

label: A mathematical approach is essential to the study of organic form
statement: A mathematical aspect of morphology, largely neglected by morphologists, is interwoven with their problems, complementary to description, and essential to the proper understanding of form.
quote: My task is finished if I have been able to shew that a certain mathematical aspect of morphology, to which as yet the morphologist gives little heed, is interwoven with his problems, complementary to his descriptive task, and helpful, nay essential, to his proper study and comprehension of Form.
scope: morphology as a science

label: Mathematical regularity and usefulness coincide in living forms
statement: What is most beautiful and regular in natural form, as in the bee's cell, is also found to be most useful and excellent.
quote: Moreover the perfection of mathematical beauty is such (as Maclaurin learned of the bee), that whatsoever is most beautiful and regular is also found to be most useful and excellent.
scope: natural forms generally, exemplified by the honeycomb

label: Living and non-living things are bound alike by physical and mathematical law
statement: Living and non-living things alike are governed by the same physical and mathematical laws.
quote: The living and the dead, things animate and inanimate, we dwellers in the world and this world wherein we dwell,—πάντα γα μὰν τὰ γιγνωσκόμενα,—are bound alike by physical and mathematical law.
scope: all living and non-living matter

label: Rules governing nature need not be those of traditional mathematics
statement: Although theoretical science requires that the systems it studies follow definite rules, those rules need not be the equation-based rules of traditional mathematics; the more general rules embodied in simple computer programs are equally candidates for describing the natural world.
quote: the crucial realization that led me to develop the new kind of science in this book is that there is in fact no reason to think that systems like those we see in nature should follow only such traditional mathematical rules.
scope: rules underlying natural systems studied by the exact sciences

label: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways
statement: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.
quote: despite the simplicity of their rules, the behavior of the programs was often far from simple. Indeed, even some of the very simplest programs that I looked at had behavior that was as complex as anything I had ever seen.
scope: simple programs such as elementary cellular automata, enumerated systematically

label: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs
statement: The great complexity seen across physical, biological and other natural systems is explained by those systems operating like typical simple programs, which commonly produce complex behavior, rather than by any special or supernatural source of complexity.
quote: For all it takes is that systems in nature operate like typical programs and then it follows that their behavior will often be complex.
scope: complex-looking physical, biological and other natural systems

label: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior
statement: Describing behavior with mathematical equations succeeds for fairly simple behavior such as planetary motion but almost inevitably fails when behavior is more complex, and descriptions based on natural selection share this limitation; thinking in terms of programs allows meaningful statements about highly complex behavior.
quote: while their basic idea of describing behavior in terms of mathematical equations works well in cases like planetary motion where the behavior is fairly simple, it almost inevitably fails whenever the behavior is more complex.
scope: traditional mathematical and evolutionary explanations in the existing sciences

label: The same basic forms of behavior recur in simple programs regardless of details
statement: Across the world of simple programs the same basic forms of behavior occur repeatedly almost independently of the underlying details of the rules, suggesting universal principles of overall behavior that should also apply to systems throughout nature.
quote: in the world of simple programs I have discovered that the same basic forms of behavior occur over and over again almost independent of underlying details.
scope: simple programs of many types (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, etc.) and, by extension, natural systems

label: Simple programs yield a straightforward explanation of thermodynamic behavior
statement: The long-standing difficulty in understanding how thermodynamic behavior, including the Second Law of Thermodynamics, arises in physics can be resolved by a straightforward explanation drawn from the behavior of simple programs.
quote: For more than a century, for example, there has been confusion about how thermodynamic behavior arises in physics. Yet from my discoveries about simple programs I have developed a quite straightforward explanation.
scope: thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, specifically the basis of entropy increase

label: A single fundamental theory of physics may be built from simple programs
statement: Thinking in terms of simple programs should make it possible to construct a single, truly fundamental theory of physics from which space, time, quantum mechanics and all other known features of the universe emerge.
quote: thinking in terms of simple programs will make it possible to construct a single truly fundamental theory of physics, from which space, time, quantum mechanics and all the other known features of our universe will emerge.
scope: the fundamental structure of the universe

label: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules
statement: Contrary to the assumption that computational universality requires elaborate systems like electronic computers, there exist systems whose rules can be stated in a single sentence that are nevertheless universal, able to perform any possible computation.
quote: there are systems whose rules are simple enough to describe in just one sentence that are nevertheless universal.
scope: simple rule systems such as elementary cellular automata and small Turing machines

label: Computational universality is far more common in abstract systems and nature
statement: Because universality can occur in systems with extremely simple rules, the phenomenon of universality is far more common and important, both among abstract systems and in nature, than previously supposed.
quote: this immediately suggests that the phenomenon of universality is vastly more common and important—in both abstract systems and nature—than has ever been imagined before.
scope: abstract rule systems and natural systems generally

label: Principle of Computational Equivalence
statement: Whenever a system in essentially any domain shows behavior that is not obviously simple, that behavior can be regarded as a computation of equivalent sophistication to that of any other such system.
quote: whenever one sees behavior that is not obviously simple—in essentially any system—it can be thought of as corresponding to a computation of equivalent sophistication.
scope: essentially all systems, abstract and natural, whose behavior is not obviously simple

label: Behavior looks complex because observers are computationally equivalent to it
statement: Simple programs appear complex to us because human perception and analysis are themselves computations that, by the Principle of Computational Equivalence, are no more sophisticated than those the programs perform.
quote: it is this equivalence between us as observers and the systems that we observe that makes the behavior of such systems seem to us complex.
scope: human perception and analysis of complex-looking systems

label: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible
statement: Predicting a system's outcome by a mathematical shortcut is normally possible only for special systems with simple behavior; other systems are computationally irreducible, so their behavior can be found only by tracing each step with roughly as much computational effort as the system itself expends.
quote: such systems are computationally irreducible—so that in effect the only way to find their behavior is to trace each of their steps, spending about as much computational effort as the systems themselves.
scope: systems whose behavior is not obviously simple

label: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules
statement: Computational irreducibility provides an explanation of how humans, even if they follow definite underlying rules, can meaningfully be said to have free will.
quote: it leads to an explanation of how we as humans—even though we may follow definite underlying rules—can still in a meaningful way show free will.
scope: human behavior and the philosophical question of free will

label: Human intelligence is computationally no more sophisticated than simple programs
statement: In terms of computation or intelligence, humans are ultimately no more sophisticated than many simple programs and many systems in nature.
quote: when it comes to computation—or intelligence—we are in the end no more sophisticated than all sorts of simple programs, and all sorts of systems in nature.
scope: human cognition compared with simple programs and natural systems

label: Complexity of simple abstract systems imposes fundamental limits on proof
statement: The complexity found in simple abstract systems leads to fundamental limitations on mathematical proof, of the kind hinted at by Gödel's Theorem, and these limitations are relevant well beyond the narrow scope of current mathematics.
quote: one of the consequences of this complexity is that it leads to fundamental limitations on the idea of proof that has been central to traditional mathematics.
scope: mathematical proof applied to abstract systems based on simple programs

label: Simple programs capture how genetic programs generate biological forms
statement: Simple programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms and appear to capture essential mechanisms by which genetic programs generate observed biological forms, enabling new models and general abstract theories in biology.
quote: such programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms—and for example seem to capture some of the essential mechanisms through which genetic programs manage to generate the actual biological forms we see.
scope: biological morphogenesis and pigmentation patterns

label: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules
statement: Contrary to engineering experience, performing sophisticated tasks does not require correspondingly complicated basic rules; extremely simple underlying rules, potentially implementable directly at the atomic scale, are often sufficient.
quote: extremely simple underlying rules—that might for example potentially be implemented directly at the level of atoms—are often all that is needed.
scope: technology and engineered systems, including nanotechnology

label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not by itself produce complexity
statement: The sensitive dependence on initial conditions studied by chaos theory only makes complexity present in the initial conditions appear in large-scale behavior; it does not imply complex behavior when initial conditions are simple.
quote: all that it shows is that if there is complexity in the details of the initial conditions, then this complexity will eventually appear in the large-scale behavior of the system.
scope: chaotic dynamical systems

label: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity
statement: Darwinian natural selection does not clearly imply the generation of complexity and in many respects tends to oppose it; a different mechanism, the intrinsic complexity of simple programs, is responsible for most great complexity in biology.
quote: I will argue in this book that in many respects it tends to oppose complexity.
scope: biological evolution and the origin of biological complexity

label: A rule-90-type cellular automaton produces a nested self-similar pattern
statement: A one-dimensional cellular automaton in which each cell becomes black when exactly one of its two neighbors was black (rule 90), started from a single black cell, produces an intricate but regular nested pattern made of triangular pieces that are smaller copies of the whole.
quote: it actually consists of many nested triangular pieces that all have exactly the same form.
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 90 from a single black cell

label: Rule 30 from a single black cell produces an irregular, complex pattern
statement: The elementary cellular automaton rule 30, started from a single black cell, produces a highly irregular and complex pattern with almost no overall regularity, rather than a uniform, repetitive or nested one.
quote: Rather than getting a simple regular pattern as we might expect, the cellular automaton instead produces a pattern that seems extremely irregular and complex.
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 30 from a single black cell

label: Simple rules with simple initial conditions can yield highly complex behavior
statement: As a general phenomenon, a system with simple underlying rules started from simple initial conditions can nevertheless show highly complex behavior.
quote: even though the underlying rules for a system are simple, and even though the system is started from simple initial conditions, the behavior that the system shows can nevertheless be highly complex.
scope: simple programs and other systems with simple rules and simple initial conditions

label: Complexity from simple rules accounts for most complexity in nature
statement: The generation of complex behavior from simple rules and simple initial conditions is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity seen in nature.
quote: I will argue that it is this basic phenomenon that is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity that we see in nature.
scope: complex phenomena throughout the natural world

label: Rule 30's center column shows no deviation from randomness over a million steps
statement: The sequence of cell colors directly below the initial black cell in rule 30 does not repeat in its first million steps, and statistical tests show no meaningful deviation from perfect randomness.
quote: in the first million steps in this sequence, for example, it never repeats, and indeed none of the tests I have ever done on it show any meaningful deviation at all from perfect randomness.
scope: center column of elementary cellular automaton rule 30 from a single black cell

label: Some cellular automata make even average properties hard to predict
statement: Some simple cellular automata, such as rule 110, are more complex than random-looking ones like rule 30: they mix regular regions with interacting localized structures, so that even average properties of their behavior become very difficult to predict.
quote: there are cellular automata whose behavior is in effect still more complex—and in which even such averages become very difficult to predict.
scope: elementary cellular automata with localized structures, especially rule 110

label: Rule 110's fate can be determined only by running it
statement: Whether the localized structures in rule 110 eventually annihilate into a regular pattern or proliferate into randomness apparently cannot be determined in advance; the only reliable method is to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as needed.
quote: The only sure way to answer these questions, it seems, is just to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as are needed
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 110 and similar systems

label: Rule 110 from one black cell becomes periodic with period 240 after about 2780 steps
statement: Rule 110 started from a single black cell resolves after about 2780 steps: one localized structure survives and interacts with periodic stripes from the left to give behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
quote: the outcome is finally clear after about 2780 steps: one structure survives, and that structure interacts with the periodic stripes coming from the left to produce behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 110 from a single black cell

label: Identical cell rules yield diverse behaviors through different configurations
statement: Even though every cell of a cellular automaton follows the same rule, different configurations of cell colors can collectively produce many different kinds of behavior, such as regular backgrounds and distinct localized structures.
quote: even though individual cells follow the same rule, different configurations of cells with different sequences of colors can together produce all sorts of different kinds of behavior.
scope: cellular automata, exemplified by rule 110

label: Intuition that complex results need complex plans comes from engineering
statement: The intuition that complex objects require complex construction plans fails because it derives from engineering, where designers restrict themselves to systems whose behavior they can understand and predict, a constraint nature does not share.
quote: Yet to do this reliably, we have to restrict ourselves to systems whose behavior we can readily understand and predict—for unless we can foresee how a system will behave, we cannot be sure that the system will do what we want.
scope: human intuition about complexity and the practice of engineering

label: Systems with simple rules and complex behavior are very common in nature
statement: Because nature is not constrained to predictable designs, systems whose simple rules produce complex behavior, like rule 30 and rule 110, are very common in nature.
quote: one of the important conclusions of this book is that such systems are actually very common in nature.
scope: natural systems generally

label: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament
statement: Historical ornamental art contains many repetitive patterns and some nested ones, but the more complicated patterns produced by simple cellular automata such as rule 30 never appear to have been used.
quote: Repetitive patterns are common and some nested patterns are seen, but the more complicated kinds of patterns discussed in this chapter do not ever appear to have been used.
scope: historical ornamental art across cultures

label: Computers enable discoveries beyond working out mathematical equations
statement: Computers are not limited to computing the consequences of mathematical equations; directly studying the behavior of even the simplest computer programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries.
quote: computers are not just limited to working out consequences of mathematical equations. And indeed, what we have seen in this chapter is that there are fundamental discoveries that can be made if one just studies directly the behavior of even some of the very simplest computer programs.
scope: the role of computers in basic science

label: Unknown phenomena are found only by systematic, preconception-free experiments
statement: Phenomena not already known to exist can be found only by very systematic and general experiments whose results are examined with as few preconceptions as possible.
quote: the only way to find phenomena that one does not already know exist is to do very systematic and general experiments, and then to look at the results with as few preconceptions as possible.
scope: scientific methodology, especially computer experiments

label: Lack of adequate computers delayed discovery of complexity from simple rules
statement: A main reason that complexity from simple programs was not discovered before the 1980s is that computer technology powerful enough for the required large-scale exploratory experiments did not yet exist, together with a lack of intuition drawn from practical computing.
quote: one of the main reasons that the discoveries I describe in this chapter were not made before the 1980s is just that computer technology did not yet exist powerful enough to do the kinds of exploratory experiments that were needed.
scope: history of science and computing

label: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do
statement: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.
quote: from experience in practical computing one knows that it is usually very difficult to foresee what even a simple program will do.
scope: simple programs, including software and cellular automata

label: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly
statement: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.
quote: The rules for generating primes are simple, yet their distribution seems in many respects random.
scope: distribution of prime numbers

label: The digits of pi appear random despite simple rules for computing them
statement: The digit sequence of pi, produced by simple computational rules, appears quite random, illustrating that simple rules can produce complex results.
quote: By the 1700s more than a hundred digits of π had been computed, and they appeared quite random.
scope: decimal digit sequence of pi

label: Complexity from simple programs was never discovered before despite many hints
statement: Although there were many hints over several centuries, including primes, digits of pi, iterated maps and the Game of Life, the basic phenomenon of simple programs producing complex behavior was never identified before Wolfram's work.
quote: despite many hints over the course of several centuries, the basic phenomenon that I have described in this chapter was never discovered before.
scope: history of science and mathematics

label: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs
statement: Whatever kind of underlying rules a simple program uses (cellular automata, mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, symbolic systems), the overall behavior that emerges falls into the same few basic types first seen in elementary cellular automata.
quote: whatever kind of underlying rules one uses, the behavior that emerges turns out to be remarkably similar to the basic examples that we have already seen in cellular automata.
scope: simple programs of all the kinds surveyed in chapter 3

label: Most elementary cellular automata give fixed-size patterns from a single black cell
statement: Among the 256 elementary (two-color, nearest-neighbor) cellular automata started from a single black cell, about two-thirds produce patterns that stay of fixed size and about one-third produce patterns that grow forever, with about 14% yielding patterns more complicated than repetition.
quote: In about two-thirds of all the cellular automata shown on the last few pages [54, 55, 56], the patterns produced remain of a fixed size. But in about one-third of cases, the patterns instead grow forever.
scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata, single-black-cell initial condition

label: Ten of the 256 elementary cellular automata produce apparent randomness
statement: Of the 256 elementary cellular automata started from a single black cell, 10 produce patterns that seem in many respects random, falling into three basic forms, while 24 produce nested patterns falling into only three fundamentally different forms.
quote: And out of the 256 rules discussed here, it turns out that 10 yield such apparent randomness. There are three basic forms, as illustrated on the facing page.
scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata, single-black-cell initial condition

label: Beyond a threshold, more complex rules do not give more complex behavior
statement: At least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules of a system does not lead to more complex overall behavior; in cellular automata, all the ingredients for the most complex behavior already exist in the elementary two-color rules.
quote: at least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules for a system does not ultimately lead to more complex overall behavior.
scope: simple programs generally, illustrated by cellular automata with more colors

label: About 85% of three-color totalistic cellular automata behave regularly
statement: About 85% of the 2187 three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular, while the remainder include rules with seemingly random behavior and rules with interacting localized structures like rule 110.
quote: About 85% of all three-color totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular.
scope: three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic cellular automata from a single gray cell

label: No basic mobile automaton shows behavior beyond repetition or nesting
statement: None of the 65,536 two-color mobile automata whose rule updates only the active cell shows behavior more complex than repetition or nesting; complex behavior appears only when the rule can also update the active cell's neighbors, and even then it is rare.
quote: Of the 65,536 possible mobile automata with rules of the kind discussed so far it turns out that not a single one shows more complex behavior.
scope: two-color mobile automata with a single active cell

label: Complex behavior correlates with many cells being active at once
statement: In generalized mobile automata, complex behavior almost never occurs unless many cells are active simultaneously, and this correlation between overall activity and complexity helps explain why complexity is much more common in cellular automata than in mobile automata.
quote: complex behavior almost never occurs except when large numbers of cells are active at the same time.
scope: mobile automata, generalized mobile automata and cellular automata

label: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting
statement: All 4096 two-state, two-color Turing machines, and all of the roughly three million three-state, two-color Turing machines started on a blank tape, ultimately produce only repetitive or nested patterns.
quote: all ultimately turn out to yield just repetitive or nested patterns—at least if they are started with all cells white.
scope: two-color Turing machines with two or three head states, blank initial tape

label: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior
statement: Two-color Turing machines with four head states can produce seemingly random behavior (about five in every million such rules), and allowing more than four states makes apparent randomness only slightly more common without changing the kinds of behavior seen.
quote: With four states, however, more complicated behavior immediately becomes possible. Indeed, in about five out of every million rules of this kind, one gets patterns with features that seem in many respects random
scope: two-color Turing machines with four or more head states, blank initial tape

label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
statement: Substitution systems in which each element is replaced according to its own color alone always produce nested patterns, so obtaining behavior more complicated than nesting requires rules that depend on at least one neighboring element.
quote: To get behavior that is more complicated than simple nesting, it follows therefore that one must consider substitution systems whose rules depend not only on the color of a single element, but also on the color of at least one of its neighbors.
scope: parallel substitution systems

label: Substitution systems with deletion need three or more colors for complexity
statement: Among two-color substitution systems that allow elements to be destroyed, those with slow growth produce only simple repetitive patterns, but allowing three or four colors immediately makes patterns as random-looking as those of cellular automata possible.
quote: allowing elements to have three or four colors rather than just two immediately makes much more complicated behavior possible.
scope: neighbor-dependent substitution systems with creation and destruction of elements

label: Text-editor-like search-and-replace rules can generate great complexity
statement: Sequential substitution systems, which repeatedly apply the first matching search-and-replace rule like a text editor, give only simple behavior with two replacements and two elements, but with three replacements about one in 10,000 random rules produces seemingly random behavior.
quote: just by using the simple operations available even in a very basic text editor, it is still ultimately possible to produce behavior of great complexity.
scope: sequential substitution (string rewriting) systems

label: One-element-deletion tag systems reduce to neighbor-independent substitution
statement: A tag system that removes only one element per step always acts as a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system and so produces only repetitive or nested patterns, whereas removing two elements per step can yield very complicated behavior.
quote: if only one element is removed at each step, then a tag system always effectively acts just like a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system of the kind we discussed on page 83.
scope: tag systems

label: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth
statement: Some cyclic tag systems with two alternating blocks, started from a single black element, produce sequences whose average growth is steady but whose fluctuations about that growth are in many respects random.
quote: if one looks at the fluctuations in this growth, as in the plots on the next page, then one finds that these fluctuations are in many respects random.
scope: cyclic tag systems with two blocks

label: Register machines need eight instructions to show complex behavior
statement: Among two-register machines with increment and decrement-jump instructions, all programs of up to four instructions behave repetitively, only two five-instruction programs give nesting, none up to seven instructions is substantially more complicated, and 126 of the 11,019,960,576 eight-instruction programs show complex behavior.
quote: But with eight instructions, 126 out of the 11,019,960,576 possible programs finally do show more complicated behavior.
scope: two-register machines with increment and decrement-jump instructions

label: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly
statement: Because register machines idealize programs in low-level languages such as C, Basic, Java or assembler, searching many millions of short programs in such languages typically yields at least a few with complex, seemingly random behavior.
quote: searching through many millions of short programs typically yields at least a few that exhibit complex and seemingly random behavior.
scope: short programs in practical low-level programming languages

label: Combinator-like symbolic rewriting systems can behave randomly
statement: Symbolic systems that repeatedly apply a single rewrite rule of the form e[x_][y_] → (expression in x and y) to nested expressions can, like other simple programs, produce behavior that is complex and seemingly random rather than stabilizing.
quote: But often—just as in so many other kinds of systems—the behavior is instead complex and seemingly quite random.
scope: combinator-like symbolic expression rewriting systems

label: Complexity does not depend on the special features of cellular automata
statement: Removing the special features of cellular automata, such as a rigid array of cells and parallel updating, does not prevent complex behavior from simple rules, so the phenomenon of complexity is universal and independent of the details of particular systems.
quote: So this suggests that in fact the phenomenon of complexity is quite universal—and quite independent of the details of particular systems.
scope: all kinds of simple programs

label: The rule-complexity threshold for complex behavior is very low
statement: Systems with sufficiently simple rules show only repetition, slightly more complicated rules often add nesting, and complex behavior requires crossing a threshold in rule complexity, but in every kind of system studied this threshold is extremely low.
quote: The remarkable discovery that we have made, however, is that this threshold is typically extremely low.
scope: all kinds of simple programs

label: Repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures dominate everywhere
statement: The four themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures are the dominant types of behavior across a vast range of systems, and these overall behavior types are almost independent of the details of the underlying rules.
quote: the basic themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures that we already saw in specific cellular automata in the previous chapter are actually very general, and in fact represent the dominant themes in the behavior of a vast range of different systems.
scope: simple programs and, by extension, a vast range of systems

label: Overall behavior of natural systems can be inferred without knowing their details
statement: Because the typical types of behavior are independent of rule details, one can make fundamental statements about the overall behavior of a natural system without knowing its internal details, and its important features will usually be ones already seen in very simple programs.
quote: even if we do not know all the details of what is inside some specific system in nature, we can still potentially make fundamental statements about its overall behavior.
scope: systems in nature

label: Computer experiments let one discover phenomena not anticipated in advance
statement: A methodology based on computer experiments, in which one runs precisely specified programs and observes their behavior, can discover genuinely unexpected phenomena that a traditional approach of constructing examples of predefined behavior would miss, while giving results as precise as mathematical statements.
quote: And the great advantage of such an experimental approach is that it does not require one to know in advance exactly what kinds of behavior can occur.
scope: methodology of studying simple programs

label: One can never start a computer experiment with too simple a system
statement: Computer experiments should study the simplest possible systems with the simplest possible procedures, because simple systems already show complex behavior, and the most common mistake is studying systems far more complicated than necessary.
quote: in my experience the single most common mistake in doing computer experiments is to look at systems that are vastly more complicated than is necessary.
scope: design of computer experiments

label: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior
statement: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.
quote: if one ignores the need for analysis and instead just looks at the results of computer experiments, then one quickly finds that even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior.
scope: simple iterative systems defined by arithmetic operations on numbers
